Solomon turns to idolatry (verses 1–8)

Few passages in Scripture give a more sorrowful or astonishing example of human corruption than this one.

Solomon became a public worshiper of detestable idols.

He probably yielded little by little to pride and luxury and lost his taste for true wisdom.

Nothing in ourselves can make us safe from the deceitfulness and corruption of the human heart.

Nor does old age remove our sinful inclinations.

Unless sinful desires are crucified and put to death through God's grace, they will never simply disappear. They can remain even when the opportunity to satisfy them is gone.

Anyone who thinks he stands securely must be careful not to fall.

Without divine grace we are weak.

Let us therefore depend continually upon that grace, stay alert and keep sober judgment.

We are fighting a dangerous battle in enemy territory, while our worst enemies are the traitors within our own hearts.

God announces judgment on Solomon (verses 9–13)

The Lord told Solomon, probably through a prophet, what his apostasy would bring upon him.

We have reason to hope Solomon repented and found mercy.

But the Holy Spirit did not expressly record his repentance.

Scripture leaves the matter uncertain, as a warning against deliberate sin.

Guilt may be forgiven while its disgrace remains.

We cannot determine before the day of judgment whether Solomon was finally left under God's everlasting displeasure.

God raises opponents against Solomon (verses 14–25)

As long as Solomon walked closely with God and kept his duty, enemies did not disturb him.

Now two adversaries rose against him.

If God is for us, even powerful opponents cannot prevail.

But if he is against us, even a small trouble can frighten us; a mere grasshopper may become a burden.

These adversaries acted from ambition or revenge.

Nevertheless, God used their actions to correct Solomon.

Jeroboam is promised the kingdom (verses 26–40)

When Ahijah explained why the kingdom would be torn from Solomon's house, he warned Jeroboam not to lose his own advancement through sin.

Yet David's house would continue, because the Messiah was to come from it.

Solomon tried to kill the man who would succeed him.

Had he not taught other people that however many plans human beings make, the Lord's counsel will stand?

Yet now Solomon himself imagined he could defeat that counsel.

Jeroboam took refuge in Egypt.

He was content for a time to live in obscurity and exile because he had the promise of a kingdom.

Should we not be equally content, when we have an even better kingdom promised to us?

Solomon dies (verses 41–43)

Solomon's reign lasted as long as his father's, but his life was shorter.

His sin shortened his days.

If earthly possessions and opportunities could satisfy the soul and bring true joy, Solomon would have found it.

Instead, they disappointed him.

He left the record of his experience to warn us: vanity and vexation of spirit.

The New Testament announces that one greater than Solomon has come to rule over us and inherit the throne of his father David.

Solomon's greatness faintly represents something of Christ's far greater excellence.

Verses 1-8
There is not a more melancholy and astonishing instance of human depravity in the sacred Scriptures, than that here recorded. Solomon became a public worshipper of abominable idols! Probably he by degrees gave way to pride and luxury, and thus lost his relish for true wisdom. Nothing forms in itself a security against the deceitfulness and depravity of the human heart. Nor will old age cure the heart of any evil propensity. If our sinful passions are not crucified and mortified by the grace of God, they never will die of themselves, but will last even when opportunities to gratify them are taken away. Let him that thinks he stands, take heed lest he fall. We see how weak we are of ourselves, without the grace of God; let us therefore live in constant dependence on that grace. Let us watch and be sober: ours is a dangerous warfare, and in an enemy's country, while our worst foes are the traitors in our own hearts. ( [1Kgs.11.9-1Kgs.11.13] 1Ki 11:9-13)
[1Kgs.11.9-1Kgs.11.13]
Verses 9-13
The Lord told Solomon, it is likely by a prophet, what he must expect for his apostacy. Though we have reason to hope that he repented, and found mercy, yet the Holy Ghost did not expressly record it, but left it doubtful, as a warning to others not to sin. The guilt may be taken away, but not the reproach; that will remain. Thus it must remain uncertain to us till the day of judgment, whether or not Solomon was left to suffer the everlasting displeasure of an offended God.
[1Kgs.11.14-1Kgs.11.25]
Verses 14-25
While Solomon kept close to God and to his duty, there was no enemy to give him uneasiness; but here we have an account of two. If against us, he can make us fear even the least, and the very grasshopper shall be a burden. Though they were moved by principles of ambition or revenge, God used them to correct Solomon.
[1Kgs.11.26-1Kgs.11.40]
Verses 26-40
In telling the reason why God rent the kingdom from the house of Solomon, Ahijah warned Jeroboam to take heed of sinning away his preferment. Yet the house of David must be supported; out of it the Messiah would arise. Solomon sought to kill his successor. Had not he taught others, that whatever devices are in men's hearts, the counsel of the Lord shall stand? Yet he himself thinks to defeat that counsel. Jeroboam withdrew into Egypt, and was content to live in exile and obscurity for awhile, being sure of a kingdom at last. Shall not we be content, who have a better kingdom in reserve?
[1Kgs.11.41-1Kgs.11.43]
Verses 41-43
Solomon's reign was as long as his father's, but his life was not so. Sin shortened his days. If the world, with all its advantages, could satisfy the soul, and afford real joy, Solomon would have found it so. But he was disappointed in all, and to warn us, has left this record of all earthly enjoyments, "Vanity and vexation of spirit." The New Testament declares that one greater than Solomon is come to reign over us, and to possess the throne of his father David. May we not see something of Christ's excellency faintly represented to us in this figure?

Rehoboam answers the people harshly (verses 1–15)

Israel's tribes complained to Rehoboam about their burdens.

They did not complain about Solomon's idolatry or his turning away from God.

Their greatest grievance should have been his religious rebellion, but they hardly cared about that as long as they could live comfortably and avoid taxes.

People inclined to division can always find something to complain about.

Considering Scripture's account of the peace, wealth and prosperity Israel enjoyed under Solomon, Henry judges their accusations to have been false or greatly exaggerated.

Rehoboam followed the advice of the younger men.

Few rulers have been more blinded by pride and the desire for arbitrary power—nothing is more destructive.

Through his foolish reply, God's prior judgment was fulfilled.

God left Rehoboam to his folly and withheld the discernment that would have led to peace, so that the kingdom would be divided.

The Lord accomplishes his wise and righteous purposes even through human errors and sins.

People who lose the kingdom of heaven likewise throw it away through stubbornness and folly, as Rehoboam threw away his kingdom.

The ten tribes rebel (verses 16–24)

The people spoke disrespectfully about David.

How quickly a good person's service to the public is forgotten!

Remembering that God governs even the losses and hardships that come to us, and that other people may be only the instruments involved, should keep us from plotting revenge.

Rehoboam and his people finally listened to the Lord's word.

When we know what God commands, we must submit even when it directly contradicts what we wanted.

If we possess God's favor, the whole universe cannot truly harm us.

Jeroboam establishes false worship (verses 25–33)

Jeroboam distrusted God's providence.

He devised his own way to protect himself and his kingship, even when doing so required sin.

Practical disbelief in God's complete sufficiency lies beneath our departures from him.

He probably intended the new worship to honor Jehovah, the God of Israel.

Yet representing God in this way violated divine law and dishonored his majesty.

People might accept worship of the God of Israel through an image more readily than openly worshiping Baal.

But that compromise paved the way for later idolatry.

Blessed Lord, give us grace to honor your temple, appointed worship, house of prayer and Sabbaths.

Never let us imitate Jeroboam by installing a detestable idol in our hearts.

Be everything precious to us.

Rule in our hearts as our hope of glory.

Verses 1-15
The tribes complained not to Rehoboam of his father's idolatry, and revolt from God. That which was the greatest grievance, was none to them; so careless were they in matters of religion, if they might live at ease, and pay no taxes. Factious spirits will never want something to complain of. And when we see the Scripture account of Solomon's reign; the peace, wealth, and prosperity Israel then enjoyed; we cannot doubt but that their charges were false, or far beyond the truth. Rehoboam answered the people according to the counsel of the young men. Never was man more blinded by pride, and desire of arbitrary power, than which nothing is more fatal. God's counsels were hereby fulfilled. He left Rehoboam to his own folly, and hid from his eyes the things which belonged to his peace, that the kingdom might be rent from him. God serves his own wise and righteous purposes by the imprudences and sins of men. Those that lose the kingdom of heaven, throw it away, as Rehoboam, by wilfulness and folly.
[1Kgs.12.16-1Kgs.12.24]
Verses 16-24
The people speak unbecomingly of David. How soon are good men, and their good services to the public, forgotten ! These considerations should reconcile us to our losses and troubles, that God is the Author of them, and our brethren the instruments: let us not meditate revenge. Rehoboam and his people hearkened to the word of the Lord. When we know God's mind, we must submit, how much soever it crosses our own mind. If we secure the favour of God, not all the universe can hurt us.
[1Kgs.12.25-1Kgs.12.33]
Verses 25-33
Jeroboam distrusted the providence of God; he would contrive ways and means, and sinful ones too, for his own safety. A practical disbelief of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all our departures from him. Though it is probable he meant his worship for Jehovah the God of Israel, it was contrary to the Divine law, and dishonourable to the Divine majesty to be thus represented. The people might be less shocked at worshipping the God of Israel under an image, than if they had at once been asked to worship Baal; but it made way for that idolatry. Blessed Lord, give us grace to reverence thy temple, thine ordinances, thine house of prayer, thy sabbaths, and never more, like Jeroboam, to set up in our hearts any idol of abomination. Be thou to us every thing precious; do thou reign and rule in our hearts, the hope of glory.

Jeroboam's altar is condemned (verses 1–10)

By threatening the altar, God's prophet also pronounced judgment upon its founder and worshipers.

False worship would not continue, but the Lord's word would remain forever.

The prophecy plainly announced that David's family would continue and support true religion, while the ten tribes would be powerless to stop what God had decreed.

When the Lord judicially hardens a sinner's heart, the person may become unable to draw back through repentance the hand that was stretched out in wrongdoing.

Such spiritual judgment, represented by Jeroboam's injured hand, is far more dreadful than a physical disability.

When Jeroboam needed help, he turned not to the golden calves, but to God's power and favor.

A time may come when people who hate faithful preaching will gladly ask faithful ministers to pray for them.

Yet Jeroboam asked only for his hand to be healed.

He did not seek pardon for his sin or a changed heart.

He was briefly impressed by both judgment and mercy, but the impression faded.

God forbade his messenger to eat or drink at Bethel to express his abhorrence of the people's idolatry and apostasy and to teach us not to share in works of darkness.

We have not learned genuine self-denial if we cannot refuse even one forbidden meal.

The prophet is deceived (verses 11–22)

The old prophet's behavior showed that he was not truly godly.

When Jeroboam changed the nation's worship, this man had preferred his comfort and interests to faithfulness.

He employed a wicked way of persuading God's messenger to return.

His story was entirely a lie.

Believers may be particularly vulnerable to temptation when disobedience comes disguised under plausible claims of holiness.

Why was the lying prophet apparently left unpunished while the faithful messenger, who was deceived, received immediate and severe judgment?

God's judgments are deeper than we can understand.

There will also be a judgment to come.

No excuse can justify deliberate disobedience.

The story illustrates the danger of listening to the great deceiver.

Those who give in to the devil when he tempts them will find him terrifying when he becomes their tormentor.

He flatters people to draw them into sin and afterward works to drive them into despair.

The disobedient prophet dies; Jeroboam does not repent (verses 23–34)

God is displeased by the sins of his own people.

Neither religious office, closeness to God nor past faithful service protects someone who willfully disobeys him.

God calls those he employs to observe his instructions strictly.

We cannot determine a person's spiritual state merely from suffering, nor measure a sin's guilt by the punishment immediately received.

For some, bodily suffering may lead to the salvation of the spirit.

For others, the body may enjoy prosperity while the soul becomes ready for judgment.

Jeroboam refused to turn from his evil way.

He believed the golden calves would secure his family's crown.

In reality, they contributed to the destruction of that crown and his house.

People who try to preserve their position through sin betray their own interests.

Let us fear success in sinful ways rather than treat it as a blessing.

Pray to be guarded against falsehood and temptation, and strengthened to follow God's commands with self-denying perseverance.

Verses 1-10
In threatening the altar, the prophet threatens the founder and worshippers. Idolatrous worship will not continue, but the word of the Lord will endure for ever. The prediction plainly declared that the family of David would continue, and support true religion, when the ten tribes would not be able to resist them. If God, in justice, harden the hearts of sinners, so that the hand they have stretched out in sin they cannot pull in again by repentance, that is a spiritual judgment, represented by this, and much more dreadful. Jeroboam looked for help, not from his calves, but from God only, from his power, and his favour. The time may come when those that hate the preaching, would be glad of the prayers of faithful ministers. Jeroboam does not desire the prophet to pray that his sin might be pardoned, and his heart changed, but only that his hand might be restored. He seemed affected for the present with both the judgment and the mercy, but the impression wore off. God forbade his messenger to eat or drink in Bethel, to show his detestation of their idolatry and apostacy from God, and to teach us not to have fellowship with the works of darkness. Those have not learned self-denial, who cannot forbear one forbidden meal.
[1Kgs.13.11-1Kgs.13.22]
Verses 11-22
The old prophet's conduct proves that he was not really a godly man. When the change took place under Jeroboam, he preferred his ease and interest to his religion. He took a very bad method to bring the good prophet back. It was all a lie. Believers are most in danger of being drawn from their duty by plausible pretences of holiness. We may wonder that the wicked prophet went unpunished, while the holy man of God was suddenly and severely punished. What shall we make of this? The judgments of God are beyond our power to fathom; and there is a judgment to come. Nothing can excuse any act of wilful disobedience. This shows what they must expect who hearken to the great deceiver. They that yield to him as a tempter, will be terrified by him as a tormentor. Those whom he now fawns upon, he will afterwards fly upon; and whom he draws into sin, he will try to drive to despair.
[1Kgs.13.23-1Kgs.13.34]
Verses 23-34
God is displeased at the sins of his own people; and no man shall be protected in disobedience, by his office, his nearness to God, or any services he has done for him. God warns all whom he employs, strictly to observe their orders. We cannot judge of men by their sufferings, nor of sins by present punishments; with some, the flesh is destroyed, that the spirit may be saved; with others, the flesh is pampered, that the soul may ripen for hell. Jeroboam returned not from his evil way. He promised himself that the calves would secure the crown to his family, but they lost it, and sunk his family. Those betray themselves who think to support themselves by any sin whatever. Let us dread prospering in sinful ways; pray to be kept from every delusion and temptation, and to be enabled to walk with self-denying perseverance in the way of God's commands.

Jeroboam sends his wife to Ahijah (verses 1–6)

When Jeroboam was doing evil, his child became sick.

When sickness enters a family, we should examine whether we have been cherishing a particular sin from which God means to turn us through this hardship.

Jeroboam would have acted more faithfully by asking why God was contending with him, requesting the prophet's prayers and throwing away his idols.

But many people would rather learn their future fortunes than hear about their faults and duties.

Jeroboam sent to Ahijah because that prophet had foretold his rise to the throne.

People who make themselves unfit to receive comfort through their sins may still expect good ministers to speak only peace to them.

In doing so they wrong both themselves and the ministers.

Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise so the prophet would answer only her question about their son.

Some people similarly try to limit their ministers to pleasant messages.

They fear hearing the full counsel of God because it might warn of judgment rather than promise comfort.

But Jeroboam's wife would learn from the prophet's first words what she must expect.

The news of a hypocrite's final portion will be dreadful.

God judges people by what they truly are, not how they appear.

Judgment is announced against Jeroboam's family (verses 7–20)

Whether or not we remember God's former mercies, he remembers them.

If we respond with ingratitude, he can bring those gifts back before us as evidence against us.

Ahijah foretold the child's approaching death.

Henry interprets this as a mercy to the child.

Of all Jeroboam's family, the boy alone showed affection for the true worship of God and disliked the worship of the calves.

God's sovereign grace can save someone from the worst household, wherever there is a genuine inclination toward the Lord God of Israel.

The righteous may be taken away from coming evil in this world and brought to the good awaiting them in a better world.

When the best member of a family dies first, it can be a warning to the others; yet death does not deprive that righteous person of any eternal blessing.

The death of the boy should have instructed both the household and the nation.

The prophet also announced judgment on Israel because its people had adopted Jeroboam's false worship.

After the ten tribes left David's house, their kingship rarely remained long in a single family.

One ruling house displaced and destroyed another.

Families and kingdoms are ruined by sin.

When influential people act wickedly, they draw others into both their guilt and its consequences.

Their condemnation is especially severe because they must answer not only for their own wrongdoing but also for the sins they encouraged others to commit and continue.

Rehoboam's evil reign (verses 21–31)

Scripture says nothing good about Rehoboam here and much that condemns the behavior of his subjects.

Jerusalem was the city God had chosen for his temple and worship.

Yet its people practiced some of the most shameful sins of the pagan nations.

This shows that nothing can transform fallen human hearts except the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit.

We should depend upon that grace and pray daily for it, for ourselves and everyone around us.

The splendor of the temple, the ceremonies of the priesthood and every outward advantage of the nation's religion could not keep the people faithful to God.

Only an outpouring of the Spirit can do that.

Sin exposes a people to danger, makes it poor and weakens it.

Shishak, king of Egypt, came and took away Jerusalem's treasures.

Sin tarnishes gold, makes what was precious grow dim and replaces it with inferior brass.

Verses 1-6
"At that time," when Jeroboam did evil, his child sickened. When sickness comes into our families, we should inquire whether there may not be some particular sin harboured in our houses, which the affliction is sent to convince us of, and reclaim us from. It had been more pious if he had desired to know wherefore God contended with him; had begged the prophet's prayers, and cast away his idols from him; but most people would rather be told their fortune, than their faults or their duty. He sent to Ahijah, because he had told him he should be king. Those who by sin disqualify themselves for comfort, yet expect that their ministers, because they are good men, should speak peace and comfort to them, greatly wrong themselves and their ministers. He sent his wife in disguise, that the prophet might only answer her question concerning her son. Thus some people would limit their ministers to smooth things, and care not for having the whole counsel of God declared to them, lest it should prophesy no good concerning them, but evil. But she shall know, at the first word, what she has to trust to. Tidings of a portion with hypocrites will be heavy tidings. God will judge men according to what they are, not by what they seem to be.
[1Kgs.14.7-1Kgs.14.20]
Verses 7-20
Whether we keep an account of God's mercies to us or not, he does; and he will set them in order before us, if we are ungrateful, to our greater confusion. Ahijah foretells the speedy death of the child then sick, in mercy to him. He only in the house of Jeroboam had affection for the true worship of God, and disliked the worship of the calves. To show the power and sovereignty of his grace, God saves some out of the worst families, in whom there is some good thing towards the Lord God of Israel. The righteous are removed from the evil to come in this world, to the good to come in a better world. It is often a bad sign for a family, when the best in it are buried out of it. Yet their death never can be a loss to themselves. It was a present affliction to the family and kingdom, by which both ought to have been instructed. God also tells the judgments which should come upon the people of Israel, for conforming to the worship Jeroboam established. After they left the house of David, the government never continued long in one family, but one undermined and destroyed another. Families and kingdoms are ruined by sin. If great men do wickedly, they draw many others, both into the guilt and punishment. The condemnation of those will be severest, who must answer, not only for their own sins, but for sins others have been drawn into, and kept in, by them.
[1Kgs.14.21-1Kgs.14.31]
Verses 21-31
Here is no good said of Rehoboam, and much said to the disadvantage of his subjects. The abounding of the worst crimes, of the worst of the heathen, in Jerusalem, the city the Lord had chosen for his temple and his worship, shows that nothing can mend the hearts of fallen men but the sanctifying grace of the Holy Spirit. On this alone may we depend; for this let us daily pray, in behalf of ourselves and all around us. The splendour of their temple, the pomp of their priesthood, and all the advantages with which their religion was attended, could not prevail to keep them close to it; nothing less than the pouring out the Spirit will keep God's Israel in their allegiance to him. Sin exposes, makes poor, and weakens any people. Shishak, king of Egypt, came and took away the treasures. Sin makes the gold become dim, changes the most fine gold, and turns it into brass.

The reign of Abijam (verses 1–8)

Abijam's heart was not wholly devoted to the Lord his God. He lacked sincerity. He began well but then fell away, walking in the sins of his father and imitating his bad example even though he had seen its harmful results.

Nevertheless, David's family remained a lamp in Jerusalem. It preserved true worship there when divine truth seemed to have been extinguished everywhere else.

The Lord continues to preserve his own cause, even when people who should have served it faithfully live and die in their sins.

The Son of David will remain a light to his church, establishing it in truth and righteousness until the end of time.

Henry distinguishes two ways of fulfilling God's law.

The first is legal fulfillment: carrying out everything the law requires through one's own obedience. Only Christ—and Adam before his fall—fulfilled it in this way.

The second is gospel fulfillment: believing in Christ, who fulfilled the law on our behalf, and sincerely endeavoring with our whole being to obey every command of God.

God accepts this obedience from everyone who is in Christ. In that sense Scripture says that David and other believers fulfilled the law.

Asa brings reform to Judah (verses 9–24)

Asa did what was right in the Lord's eyes. What God judges to be right is right indeed.

His reign was a period of reform.

Reformation begins by removing evil, and Asa found a great deal of evil to remove.

When idolatry was present within his own royal household, he removed it there too.

Reformation must begin at home.

He respected and loved his mother, but loved God more.

People who possess authority are blessed when they have hearts willing to use it well.

Yet we must not merely stop doing evil; we must also learn to do good.

We should not only throw away our sinful idols but dedicate ourselves and all we possess to God's glory.

Asa was sincerely committed to serving God. His sins did not come from a presumptuous desire to rebel.

But his alliance with Ben-hadad arose from unbelief.

Even genuine believers find it hard to trust the Lord wholeheartedly in urgent danger.

Unbelief makes room for worldly schemes, and one sin can lead to another.

Christians have sometimes sought help from the Lord's enemies in their disputes with their own brothers and sisters.

In this way, people who once shone brightly may find their final years clouded over.

Nadab and Baasha rule Israel (verses 25–34)

During Asa's single reign in Judah, Israel's government passed into six or seven different hands.

Notice the destruction of Jeroboam's family.

Not one word of God will fall to the ground.

His warnings of judgment are not spoken merely to frighten people without consequence.

Wicked people sometimes carry out God's righteous judgments against one another.

Yet amid dreadful sins and apparent confusion, the Lord continues fulfilling his own plan.

When that plan is finally complete, his glorious justice, wisdom, truth and mercy will be admired and worshiped forever.
classic_reading:
[1Kgs.15.1-1Kgs.15.8]
Chapter 15
Chapter Outline
Wicked reign of Abijam, king of Judah. | (1-8) |
Good reign of Asa, king of Judah. | (9-24) |
The evil reigns of Nadab and Baasha in Israel. | (25-34) |
Verses 1-8
Abijam's heart was not perfect with the Lord his God; he wanted sincerity; he began well, but he fell off, and walked in all the sins of his father, following his bad example, though he had seen the bad consequences of it. David's family was continued as a lamp in Jerusalem, to maintain the true worship of God there, when the light of Divine truth was extinguished in all other places. The Lord has still taken care of his cause, while those who ought to have been serviceable thereto have lived and perished in their sins. The Son of David will still continue a light to his church, to establish it in truth and righteousness to the end of time. There are two kinds of fulfilling the law, one legal, the other by the gospel. Legal is, when men do all things required in the law, and that by themselves. None ever thus fulfilled the law but Christ, and Adam before his fall. The gospel manner of fulfilling the law is, to believe in Christ who fulfilled the law for us, and to endeavour in the whole man to obey God in all his precepts. And this is accepted of God, as to all those that are in Christ. Thus David and others are said to fulfil the law.
[1Kgs.15.9-1Kgs.15.24]
Verses 9-24
Asa did what was right in the eyes of the Lord. That is right indeed which is so in God's eyes. Asa's times were times of reformation. He removed that which was evil; there reformation begins, and a great deal he found to do. When Asa found idolatry in the court, he rooted it out thence. Reformation must begin at home. Asa honours and respects his mother; he loves her well, but he loves God better. Those that have power are happy when thus they have hearts to use it well. We must not only cease to do evil, but learn to do well; not only cast away the idols of our iniquity, but dedicate ourselves and our all to God's honour and glory. Asa was cordially devoted to the service of God, his sins not arising from presumption. But his league with Benhadad arose from unbelief. Even true believers find it hard, in times of urgent danger, to trust in the Lord with all their heart. Unbelief makes way for carnal policy, and thus for one sin after another. Unbelief has often led Christians to call in the help of the Lord's enemies in their contests with their brethren; and some who once shone brightly, have thus been covered with a dark cloud towards the end of their days.

The Lord gave him an answer. He declares that the wicked house of Ahab shall be rooted out, that the people of Israel shall be punished for their sins; and he shows that Elijah was not left alone as he had supposed, and also that a helper should at once be raised up for him. Thus all his complaints are answered and provided for. God's faithful ones are often his hidden ones, [Ps.83.3] Psa 83:3, and the visible church is scarcely to be seen: the wheat is lost in chaff, and the gold in dross, till the sifting, refining, separating day comes. The Lord knows them that are his, though we do not; he sees in secret. When we come to heaven we shall miss many whom we thought to have met there; we shall meet many whom we little thought to have met there. God's love often proves larger than man's charity, and far more extended.
[1Kgs.19.19-1Kgs.19.21]
Verses 19-21
Elijah found Elisha by Divine direction, not in the schools of the prophets, but in the field; not reading, or praying, or sacrificing, but ploughing. Idleness is no man's honour, nor is husbandry any man's disgrace. An honest calling in the world, does not put us out of the way of our heavenly calling, any more than it did Elisha. His heart was touched by the Holy Spirit, and he was ready to leave all to attend Elijah. It is in a day of power that Christ's subjects are made willing; nor would any come to Christ unless they were thus drawn. It was a discouraging time for prophets to set out in. A man that had consulted with flesh and blood, would not be fond of Elijah's mantle; yet Elisha cheerfully leaves all to accompany him. When the Saviour said to one and to another, Follow me, the dearest friends and most profitable occupations were cheerfully left, and the most arduous duties done from love to his name. May we, in like manner, feel the energy of his grace working in us mightily, and by unreserved submission at once, may we make our calling and election sure.

Verses 1-11
Benhadad sent Ahab a very insolent demand. Ahab sent a very disgraceful submission; sin brings men into such straits, by putting them out of the Divine protection. If God do not rule us, our enemies shall: guilt dispirits men, and makes them cowards. Ahab became desperate. Men will part with their most pleasant things, those they most love, to save their lives; yet they lose their souls rather than part with any pleasure or interest to prevent it. Here is one of the wisest sayings that ever Ahab spake, and it is a good lesson to all. It is folly to boast of any day to come, since we know not what it may bring forth. Apply it to our spiritual conflicts. Peter fell by self-confidence. Happy is the man who is never off his watch.
[1Kgs.20.12-1Kgs.20.21]
Verses 12-21
The proud Syrians were beaten, and the despised Israelites were conquerors. The orders of the proud, drunken king disordered his troops, and prevented them from attacking the Israelites. Those that are most secure, are commonly least courageous. Ahab slew the Syrians with a great slaughter. God often makes one wicked man a scourge to another.
[1Kgs.20.22-1Kgs.20.30]
Verses 22-30
Those about Benhadad advised him to change his ground. They take it for granted that it was not Israel, but Israel's gods, that beat them; but they speak very ignorantly of Jehovah. They supposed that Israel had many gods, to whom they ascribed limited power within a certain district; thus vain were the Gentiles in their imaginations concerning God. The greatest wisdom in worldly concerns is often united with the most contemptible folly in the things of God.
[1Kgs.20.31-1Kgs.20.43]
Verses 31-43
This encouragement sinners have to repent and humble themselves before God; Have we not heard, that the God of Israel is a merciful God? Have we not found him so? That is gospel repentance, which flows from an apprehension of the mercy of God, in Christ; there is forgiveness with him. What a change is here! The most haughty in prosperity often are most abject in adversity; an evil spirit will thus affect a man in both these conditions. There are those on whom, like Ahab, success is ill bestowed; they know not how to serve either God or their generation, or even their own true interests with their prosperity: Let favour be showed to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness. The prophet designed to reprove Ahab by a parable. If a good prophet were punished for sparing his friend and God's when God said, Smite, of much sorer punishment should a wicked king be thought worthy, who spared his enemy and God's, when God said, Smite. Ahab went to his house, heavy and displeased, not truly penitent, or seeking to undo what he had done amiss; every way out of humour, notwithstanding his victory. Alas! many that hear the glad tidings of Christ, are busy and there till the day of salvation is gone.
